domains.title: Castle City of the Chūbu Heartland
domains.subtitle: Commerce, Craft, and Tokugawa Power
domains.lead: Nagoya is Japan's fourth-largest city and a historic center of commerce and craftsmanship. Built around the castle commissioned by Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1612, Nagoya grew into a hub of ceramics, textiles, automotive manufacturing, and trade. Its name, 'peaceful ancient house,' reflects a city that has long served as a stable crossroads.

mythology.lead: Nagoya's mythology is more historical than divine: a castle city built by samurai and grown by merchants.

myths.title: The Building of Nagoya Castle
myths.text: In 1612, Tokugawa Ieyasu ordered the construction of Nagoya Castle to secure the strategic Chūbu region and to house his son Yoshinao. The castle was built with materials from Sunpu and Kiyosu, and its golden shachihoko became a symbol of Tokugawa wealth and vigilance.

myths.title: The Peaceful Ancient House
myths.text: The name Nagoya is traditionally explained as deriving from the shrine of Nagoya in the old Owari province, meaning 'peaceful ancient house' or 'prosperous ancient house.' The name predates the castle and reflects the area's long settlement history.

myths.title: From Castle Town to Industrial City
myths.text: Nagoya transformed from a castle town into one of Japan's great industrial cities. Toyota and other manufacturers made the region synonymous with Japanese industry, while the castle and its festivals preserved the city's samurai heritage.

lore.syncretism: Nagoya sits at the intersection of samurai, merchant, and industrial Japan. Its castle expresses Tokugawa military architecture; its crafts draw on medieval guild traditions; and its modern economy powers the nation's manufacturing. The city is less a mythic symbol than a practical crossroads that accumulated meaning over centuries.
lore.culturalLegacy: Nagoya is known today for its castle, its food, and its industrial might. The reconstructed castle keep attracts millions, and the city's cuisine has a national reputation. Nagoya's role as a transportation and manufacturing hub makes it a pillar of contemporary Japan.
lore.extendedMeditation: Nagoya reminds us that not sacred places begin as holy mountains. Some become important simply by being where roads meet, where castles rise, and where people gather to make things. The golden shachihoko on the castle roof watch over a city built on work.
lore.archaeology: Nagoya Castle, originally completed in 1615 and reconstructed in concrete in 1959, is the city's dominant historical site. Excavations in the castle grounds and the older Kiyosu area have revealed medieval and early modern settlement layers. The region's ceramic kilns and industrial sites document its transformation into a manufacturing center.
